title: RJ Mitte, ‘Breaking Bad’ Star, Dies at 34

body:
RJ Mitte, who played Walter White Jr. on “Breaking Bad,” has died. He was 34.

	A representative for Mitte confirmed the news to Variety. A cause of death was not immediately disclosed.

	Like his “Breaking Bad” character Walt Jr., Mitte had cerebral palsy. Throughout his acting career, he was an advocate for disability representation in Hollywood.


	“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” a representative for Mitte said in a statement. “Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.” 
	

	Mitte served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s, and he was the president of his own charity, the Mitte Foundation, which supported various philanthropic efforts while challenging stereotypes about people with disabilities.

	Mitte also played Mind Master in the Netflix superhero series “The Guardians of Justice.” His credits also include 2017’s “The Recall” and 2020’s “The Oak Room.”

	He had been dating Kennedy Suarez since 2018 and announced their engagement in 2025.

	If you or anyone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline by dialing 988 or go to SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

title: How ‘Ink’ Production Designers Recreated The Sun Newsroom Using Functional Linotype Machines, Working Rotary Phones and Old Typewriters
description:
Danny Boyle’s latest film “Ink” traces the rise of Rupert Murdoch on London’s Fleet Street and the takeover of The Sun newspaper.

	The film premier
body:
Danny Boyle’s latest film “Ink” traces the rise of Rupert Murdoch on London’s Fleet Street and the takeover of The Sun newspaper.

	The film premieres at the London Film Festival and will open in select theaters Dec. 11 before landing on Netflix on Jan. 8 in the U.S. and Latin America.

	“Ink” is based on the Tony-nominated play of the same name by James Graham, who adapted his own work for the screen. Guy Pearce plays a brash, 30-something Rupert Murdoch, with Jack O’Connell as editor Larry Lamb, the working-class newspaper journalist who helped him remake The Sun into a populist juggernaut.
	

	Set in 1969 London, Boyle enlisted his go-to production designers, Gareth Pugh and Carson McColl, to bring his vision to life. Boyle’s brief was simple. “He said he wanted to reset the expectations of a period film,” McColl explains. “We took that to mean that he wanted to recreate 1969, but in a way that felt immediate and grabby.” They looked back at how The Sun was one of the original places to find clickbait-style headlines. 


	Fleet Street



	

									Anthony Dickenson
	



	The Fleet Street of today looks vastly different from the Fleet Street of 1969. “A lot of Fleet Street doesn’t exist anymore,” Pugh says. 

	The Sun’s 1969 headquarters was originally located on Bouverie Street, with the print press set in the basement of the offices. In its place now stand modern buildings. “We ran into challenges when trying to recreate the newsroom,” Pugh says. 

	They ultimately found a space in Bromley, U.K., which they could transform for filming. “It had been vacated by the local council, and the mix of different architectural styles made it ideal for housing the various set-pieces, particularly the newsroom,” he explains.
	

	The Newsroom



	

									Anthony Dickenson
	



	The newsroom was a huge undertaking for Pugh, and McColl describes it as the “nerve center” of the film.

	Boyle referred to the space as a spaceship.  Pugh notes, “It’s where we spent most of our time in the script.” 

	McColl adds, “For the space to feel real, the layout was key. In a newsroom, especially of that era, there was a daily system of way-finding — from the morning until the copy deadline at night — that would escalate into a frenzy of activity and human traffic.” He explains they worked with consultants who had experience on Fleet Street in 1969 to map out the newsroom and choreograph its flow with the cast. “It was amazing to see how it resembled an ecosystem,” McColl says.

	The set had to balance breadth and scale despite the film’s low budget, which forced the team to be both creative and resourceful. “Danny gives us a lot of latitude when we’re designing sets,” McColl says.

	The pair had recently given up smoking, but they wanted to add an extra layer of authenticity. McColl says, “We smoked like two packets of cigarettes, so that it smelled like cigarette smoke.” 

	In addition to that, they found old rotary phones, typewriters and other set-pieces that immersed the cast and the film in that era.



	

									Anthony Dickenson
	



	Linotype Machines

	One challenge was finding the Linotype machines which The Sun relied on for its typesetting. McColl says, “They’re priceless. There are very, very few left in the world.”

	The film’s set decorator Ben Barrington Groves came to the rescue. McColl says, “He found someone who had an obsession with hot metal printing and he convinced them to come on this journey with us.” The team ultimately secured three fully functional Linotype machines.

	Larry’s Office

	Larry Lamb’s office was designed to reflect the arc of his story. McColl explains, “The newsroom was supposed to look tired — functional, but reflective of a struggling newspaper. Amid the chaos, Larry needed his own space and as the movie progresses, he should feel increasingly isolated. We wanted the audience to see him through the gridded glass windows, alone in the final scenes where he’s on the phone with Hugh Cudlip, the newsroom deserted. It was a visual way of showing that while he got everything he wanted, he’s found himself alone.”
	

	The team also worked closely with set decorator, Alice Davies, whose contributions proved invaluable. “When I walked into Larry’s office one day, her rough layout was nearly perfect,” McColl recalls. “It was a testament to how closely attuned we were to one another.”

	So much was their eye and attention for detail that they found a way to make Larry’s phone work. “You could pick it up and you’d get the sales numbers,” McColl says.



	

					Costume designer Carson McColl and production designer Gareth Pugh on the set of “Ink.”
									Anthony Dickenson
	



	The Tube

	In one sequence, Rupert Murdoch is riding the tube. As with everything else, London Underground had since been modernized. So, the train sequence presented its own challenges. “There’s only one train of the right era, located near Watford,” Pugh explains. “It’s part of a museum, so the idea of bringing a film crew in initially made the curators nervous.”

	When it couldn’t be used how they wanted, they got creative. Pugh says, “We used high-powered wind machines and flying newspapers to create the frenetic environment, all while being careful with the artifacts.”

	The scene was brought to life by lighting designer Steve Mackie, who used fast-moving bar lights. “He was able to rush light down the entire length of the train and make it look like it was going at a million miles an hour,” Pugh says.

	McColl adds, “There was something very punk and DIY. During prep, we experimented with different setups — running cameras down corridors and building fake tube windows to achieve the right look. Danny brought a 360-degree camera into ‘Ink,’ and used it for certain sequences, including the pivotal kidnapping of Muriel Mackay. It felt brave and risky, but it paid off.”



	

					INK. (L to R) Jonathan Hyde as Sir Alick McKay and Jack OConnell as Lamb in INK. Cr. Courtesy of Studiocanal © 2026.

title: Grace Helbig Reveals Upcoming Surgery for Brain Tumors Three Years After Beating Breast Cancer
description:
Grace Helbig is dealing with cancer for a second time.

	On Monday, the YouTuber and comedian posted a video on Instagram in which she shared that a
body:
Grace Helbig is dealing with cancer for a second time.

	On Monday, the YouTuber and comedian posted a video on Instagram in which she shared that after going to the emergency room because of numbness in her legs, doctors found two tumors in her brain. “She missed me. My cancer missed me. Why wouldn’t she want to be in my body?”

	Helbig will undergo brain surgery to remove the tumors on Wednesday, she said. “I feel very positive and optimistic because these are operable brain tumors, and there was a moment in time where it wasn’t certain. Quite scary.” She went on to explain that she and frequent collaborator Mamrie Hart would be cancelling all 2026 dates of their podcast tour, “This Might Get Weird,” and rescheduling them for 2027. “Obviously, we’ll take this week off of podcasting, but trust me, there’ll be plenty of stories for the next podcast, when that happens,” Helbig added.
	

	Helbig was diagnosed with triple-positive breast cancer in the summer of 2023 after noticing a small lump in her breast. “Get those lumps checked,” she said at the time. “And don’t be afraid to ask the doctor what you think might be a stupid question.” 


	Helbig has approached both diagnoses with humor. “I’ve asked the doctors. They said the positive attitude can’t fix it, but it can help,” she joked in Monday’s video. In 2023, amid her first round of treatment, she said, “There’s some humor to be found here. The joke’s not lost on me that I’ve spent 15 years not using my boobs to get attention on the internet, and yet here we are. And that I’m announcing this during Cancer season. So what’s next? This is my job now and I’m going to fight this little bitch of a thing in my left breast as best and as strongly and as gracefully as I can. Pun intended.”

schema.headline: Grace Helbig Reveals Upcoming Surgery for Brain Tumors Three Years After Beating Breast Cancer

title: Like Its Hero, Marvel’s ‘VisionQuest’ Struggles to Connect Emotionally: TV Review
description: Partway through “VisionQuest,” the titular android Vision (Paul Bettany) attempts to help a British teenager named Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) understan
body:
Partway through “VisionQuest,” the titular android Vision (Paul Bettany) attempts to help a British teenager named Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) understand the precise nature of their relationship. The truth goes something like this: Vision is a reconstituted version of his former self, who was killed by Thanos in “Avengers: Infinity War” and then kinda-sorta brought back sans memories by his wife Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen), a grieving witch, in the 2021 series “WandaVision”; Tommy is an ordinary person suddenly imbued with the consciousness and abilities of a child Wanda invented with magic, which survived the collapse of his mother’s suburban simulation and crossed the pond in search of a host.
	

	Vision runs a simulation where he struggles, over and over again, to condense all this lore and explain it to Tommy in a way that doesn’t overwhelm him with anger and confusion. There’s not a single version that doesn’t end with Tommy storming out of the room.


	This is more or less how it feels to watch “VisionQuest,” an eight-episode Marvel Studios series that’s positioned as a sequel of sorts to “WandaVision.” The show plays with some clever concepts, particularly in its visual presentation; as the simulation scenarios pile up, so do Vision clones until a dozen exhausted, exasperated Bettanys all collapse on a hotel floor. (Much of “VisionQuest” strips away the monochrome coating to show Vision as an ordinary human, allowing Bettany to flex his fusty charm.) But this imagery is larded with so much convoluted backstory and abstract concepts that “VisionQuest” ends up in the exact same predicament as Vision himself, a synthetic being trying and mostly failing to connect with his emotions.
	

	Artificial intelligence has long been a staple of comics and other forms of science fiction, but as real-life AI companies talk seriously about potential sentience, there’s a topical slant to Vision’s preferred strategy for getting in touch with his feelings. He’s created and/or convened a bunch of autonomous AIs — what we would now call “agents,” though creator Terry Matalas may have overseen the scripts before that term fully entered the popular lexicon — to help him with various tasks. There’s F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), who helps decode social interactions, and E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), who’s a proponent of fun. Mechanics D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis) and U (Jonathan Sayer) tend to the more mundane work of keeping internal systems in shape. Finally, there are more familiar figures from earlier stages of the MCU: Tony Stark’s old pal J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy) is on hand; most intriguingly, so is Ultron (James Spader), the namesake antagonist of the second “Avengers” film.

	All these assistants take corporeal form in Vision’s so-called Mindspace, a virtual and psychological plane that takes the shape of a quirky Victorian mansion. Here, Ultron looks not like a menacing CGI robot but the 66-year-old Spader himself: a schlubby guy with a flowing beard and a trenchcoat whose menacing, purple-prosed monologues (“It feels to me like your Greek tragedy has a deuteragonist”) are undercut by his appearance. To the show’s credit, this Ultron is a highly entertaining creation, allowing Spader to layer some of his signature sardonic air to a character who’s still cynical, but much humbled from his supervillain days. Without access to the real world, Ultron has to settle for being the devil on Vision’s shoulder rather than an actor in his own right.

	It’s when the Mindspace intersects with said real world that “VisionQuest” gets overly complicated. Directors Christopher J. Byrne, Gandja Monteiro and Vincenzo Natali — along with Matalas, who helms the final pair of episodes — have some fun inside that mutable dimension: When a hostile android’s neural network connects with Vision’s, the episode becomes a riff on possession and exorcism (“The power of code compels you!”), and when Ultron begs Vision to let him “take the wheel,” it’s a literal ship’s wheel buffeted by stormwinds. But apart from having the AIs appear and speak to Vision as a kind of imaginary friend, invisible to everyone else, “VisionQuest” never lands on a consistent or legible way to map the relationship between the two realms, or how events in one affect the material reality of the other.
	

	Constantly toggling between the Mindspace and meatspace (sorry, it’s right there!) inevitably takes a toll on Tommy, who only exists in the latter. Even by the fantastical standards of comics-based storytelling, the tenuousness of Tommy’s nature — he’s kind of another incarnation of Quicksilver, played by Evan Peters in “WandaVision,” but also kind of not? — makes him a difficult protagonist to map onto. That straining to comprehend the irrational fog of human emotions is the show’s explicit subject only clarifies the problem rather than neutralizing it. As Vision wonders what his purpose is without Wanda or the Avengers, we do, too.

	“VisionQuest” tries to balance such philosophical questions about consciousness (yes, the Ship of Theseus metaphor comes back) with more active conflicts. At the behest of a mysterious client, the bounty hunter Paladin (Todd Stashwick) is on Vision’s trail, as is the aforementioned android (T’Nia Miller). Evading them provides some momentum, though not enough to propel an entire cast so massive I haven’t even mentioned Diane “Philomena Cunk” Morgan, who plays the Paladin’s assistant, yet. Before long, “VisionQuest” is trying to stitch all its unwieldy threads together with basic clichés about chosen family. “VisionQuest” often tells the audience what we’re supposed to be feeling, yet rarely achieves its stated aim.

	“WandaVision” was the first Marvel Studios show to air on Disney+, and with its shapeshifting sitcom homage as an allegory for grief, that series has remained a high bar to beat amid the MCU’s oversaturation era. This remains the case for the direct sequel. “VisionQuest” rehashes many of the same themes about recovering from loss — there is, of course, a flashback to the famous line about love persevering — with a hero who is, by definition, much less accessible. (And given AI’s alarming trajectory toward mass job replacement and/or civilizational destruction, I didn’t feel especially inclined to empathize with a bunch of digital entities.) “VisionQuest” can be enjoyable in its comfort zone of zanily tweaking the Mindspace. But when it’s time to venture out into the tactile world, the show doesn’t leave a lasting mark.

	The first two episodes of “VisionQuest” will premiere on Disney+ on Oct. 14, with remaining episodes airing weekly on Wednesdays.

schema.headline: Like Its Hero, Marvel’s ‘VisionQuest’ Struggles to Connect Emotionally: TV Review

title: Ben Affleck Calls ‘Justice League’ Reshoots the ‘Low Point of My Career’: ‘It Was So Gross’ How the Studio Replaced Zack Snyder With Joss Whedon
description: Ben Affleck appeared on the latest episode of the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast and called the reshoots for “Justice League” the “low point of my car
body:
Ben Affleck appeared on the latest episode of the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast and called the reshoots for “Justice League” the “low point of my career.” 

	Warner Bros. infamously replaced director Zack Snyder with Joss Whedon to overhaul the movie after Snyder needed to pause work due to his daughter’s death. Snyder estimated in a recent interview with Variety that Whedon’s reshoots covered 60 new pages of material. The end product resulted in a critical and commercial misfire for Warner Bros. Whedon was later accused by “Justice League” actor Gal Gadot of threatening her on set, claims of which he denied.
	

	“The experience of ‘Justice League’ was so negative for lots of different reasons, some of which have to do with where I was at personally and some of which had to do with the tragedy that happened at that time,” Affleck said. “I saw how not to make a movie like that, which is where the studio is at odds with the filmmaker. You are really making a mistake. I was really glad and gratified that Zack got to release [his version via the Snyder Cut]. That was fucking great. I was really happy for him. That was shitty, him being taken off that movie and the reshoots that we did. If you want the low point of my career, it was that.”


	“Somebody’s death by suicide eclipses everything,” Affleck continued, referring to the death of Snyder’s daughter. “The way in which that was, I thought, used as an excuse [to replace Zack] was one of the shittiest things I’ve ever seen. It was so gross. The whole environment and vibe [on set during the reshoots], much of which I was not privy to but heard secondhand from the actors, it was just, ‘Wow, this is about as gross as it gets.’ And I was drinking too much… and I got divorced. It was a difficult time for me personally, but those thing, while painful, did not impact that movie.”
	

	Affleck previously told Entertainment Weekly that making “Justice League” was “a nadir experience” that made him not want to continue playing Batman. The actor added at the time: “I didn’t like being there. I didn’t think it was interesting. And then some really shitty things, awful things happened. But, that’s when I was like, I’m not going to do that anymore.”

	Elsewhere during his “Happy Sad Confused” interview, Affleck confirmed that Lucasfilm approached him about directing “Star Wars: The Force Awakens.” Whether that means he was the studio’s first choice or if they were also talking to eventual pick J.J. Abrams at the time is not something Affleck knows. 

	“I talked to those folks at the time, and that was one where I just was like, again, I thought like, ‘Hey, I like ‘Star Wars’ and I’m a fan, but I’m not the person to direct this movie,’” Affleck explained about turning down “Star Wars.” 

	“I just think someone else who has more passion for this is going to do a better job. There’s a lot of challenges to reinventing that,” Affleck continued. “In fact, you’ve seen that played out. It hasn’t been easy for them to reinvent that franchise. Some have done really well, some — and you’ve got this whole fan base that’s got its own very strong opinions… I just thought like, ‘You know what? This would be — I don’t think I can do it as well as somebody else, and I don’t want to direct something that I don’t feel like I have a chance to be really really proud of.’”

	Watch Affleck’s full interview on “Happy Sad Confused” below.

schema.headline: Ben Affleck Calls ‘Justice League’ Reshoots the ‘Low Point of My Career’: ‘It Was So Gross’ How the Studio Replaced Zack Snyder With Joss Whedon

title: Tilly Nollywood? African Filmmakers — Ready or Not — Get Set for the AI Revolution
description: The world premiere of what’s been billed as the first photorealistic, AI-generated feature film in the Yoruba language fizzled out last week when us
body:
The world premiere of what’s been billed as the first photorealistic, AI-generated feature film in the Yoruba language fizzled out last week when user demand overwhelmed the servers of Docuth, the streaming platform that hosted the launch.

	After months of hype building to the release of “Asiri Ilu Awon Osu” (Mystery of Osu Land), the film’s Nigerian producers, Mysterious Tech Studio, took to social media to apologize for the glitch, telling their followers: “To everyone at home and abroad who has tried to watch and could not get through, please do not be offended or discouraged.”
	

	The episode felt somehow symbolic for this moment in the history of AI in Africa, where excitement over the technology’s transformative potential for the continent’s filmmakers often runs counter to the practical realities on the ground.


	As African industry professionals convened at this year’s Durban FilmMart, both the potential and pitfalls of artificial intelligence were high on the agenda.

	Among the chief concerns for many stakeholders are the barriers to entry. AI tools that are widely available elsewhere in the world face unique challenges in reaching African consumers, from high data costs and low broadband speeds to payment-processing headaches.

	Tamara Dawit, of Ethiopian Canadian production company Gobez Media, noted that those challenges represent significant “systemic barriers” to the adoption of the latest tech tools on the African continent.

	“How do we address those issues so that everyone is benefitting from the advancements in technology?” she said. “If these are great opportunities for the industry, can everybody actually access them?”
	

	Zukisani Karabo Mabece, of media-tech and production company Digicine Motion Picture, agreed. 

	“AI isn’t necessarily a magic pill,” said Mabece, whose Johannesburg-based company has leaned into generative AI with a host of digital tools designed to democratize access to cutting-edge technology for African filmmakers.

	“It’s very biased. It’s very Western,” he said. “We’re having to build our own language models to accommodate the languages that we have here locally. We took it upon ourselves to build models that serve our market and our geography.”

	In some instances, the rapid adoption of AI technology has had unintended consequences that aren’t unique to Africa. 

	Earlier this year, the South African government drafted an ambitious AI policy that was summarily withdrawn when journalists discovered that at least six of its 67 academic citations were the by-products of AI hallucinations, referring to journals and authors that did not exist. The drafters appeared to have used a large-language model to compose the policy without verifying its claims.

	While the blunder was a PR disaster for South African policymakers, Amilcar Patel, who serves as co-chair of the South African Screen Federation (SASFED), noted that there are more pernicious dangers lurking for Africans when it comes to using AI tools developed in the Global North.

	“We need to be very careful when we’re using AI in our work, especially in our policy and legal work, because we’re infusing a very different culture that doesn’t protect women, that doesn’t protect the poor, that doesn’t protect the vulnerable, into our legislative framework,” said Patel. “And then it becomes law.”

	For African creatives, there are additional ethical factors to consider. 

	“AI mirrors society,” said Dawit. “Society has a lot of systemic inequities within it, and those show up [in AI models].”

	“Those that are building AI don’t look like us. Biases are already built into the AI systems,” added Samantha Kaine, of the Independent Media Producers Assn. of Creative Talent (I.M.P.A.C.T.). “When the major AI models are trained largely on Western data and Western culture, what does it take to use these tools without importing someone else’s aesthetic or erasing who we are — erasing our own identity?”
	

	Such concerns are likely to be on the agenda next month when Cape Town plays host to the Africa AI Summit, a three-day event that gathers heads of state and global tech and business leaders to draw up a roadmap that will shape the future of AI across Africa and the Global South.

	Backed by partners including the World Bank, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Nvidia, the event is built around a billion-dollar AI initiative that’s designed to accelerate the deployment of artificial intelligence across the continent.

	In the meantime, African filmmakers will continue to find uses for AI tools, even as the continent’s digital infrastructure and policy frameworks are forced to play catch-up.

	One week after the failed rollout of “Mystery of Osu Land,” Kafilat Yusuff, of Mysterious Tech Studio, told Variety that after “viewers experienced intermittent access due to high traffic at launch,” the platform “has now been stabilized.” The film, which incorporated roughly 80% AI-assisted scenes with 20% live-action scenes utilizing real actors and their voices, is now available to stream on Docuth.

	“Our experience has shown us that AI offers independent African filmmakers new ways to explore ambitious stories and visual worlds,” Yusuff said. “However, it also raises important questions about the role of human performers, consent, compensation, creative ownership and how audiences receive AI-assisted films.”

	As for future plans, she said that the company is holding off on a follow-up until “Mystery of Osu Land” has had time to enjoy a “full run.”

	“We spent a lot of time building this, and with the premiere traffic we just saw on Docuth, it’s clear there’s a lot of global curiosity. So our focus now is festivals, wider press and securing a stable global streaming release so everyone who wants to see it can,” she said.

	“We are documenting everything we learned from this hybrid 80% AI-20% live-action pipeline, which will eventually help us and other African filmmakers make future projects at lower cost.”

	The Durban FilmMart runs Oct. 9 – 12 in Durban, South Africa.

schema.headline: Tilly Nollywood? African Filmmakers — Ready or Not — Get Set for the AI Revolution

title: Katherine Mallen Kupferer, Audrey Grace Marshall, Dean Norris, Jordan Ladd Join ‘The Attentionist’ from Caroline Kepnes (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Caroline Kepnes, author of the novel series “You,” which inspired the global Netflix hit, has assembled a team of buzzy actors for her series direct
body:
Caroline Kepnes, author of the novel series “You,” which inspired the global Netflix hit, has assembled a team of buzzy actors for her series directorial debut.

	Katherine Mallen Kupferer, Audrey Grace Marshall, Dean Norris and Jordan Ladd will star in “The Attentionist,” a digital-first project that combines elements of a ’90s family dramedy and a psychological thriller. 

	Kupferer and Marshall will play sisters Maeve and Reg, whose sibling dynamic is “gloriously messy,” according to an official description. The two actors just co-starred in “Mouse,” a Berlin Film Festival player this year starring Sophie Okonedo and David Hyde Pierce.
	

	Norris (a fan favorite from “Breaking Bad”) and Ladd (a noted scream queen) play their parents. Norris’ character is “Tony Soprano minus the Mafia,” while Ladd’s plays an “unfairly hot mom not aware her daughters are unraveling.”


	“The Attentionist” is set in a ‘90s Cape Cod neighborhood where the coastal elite live side by side with seasonal summer residents. The story picks up when 14-year-old Maeve and her older sister, Reg, start a secret phone romance with a boy from the local boat club who promises a way into the upper echelons of Cape Cod society. But when the voice on the phone takes a dark turn, Maeve keeps listening, pulling her family further into a monstrous secret.

	Kepnes serves as writer and director for “The Attentionist.” Mark Roberts of Roberts Media (“Meet Me Next Christmas”) and Lorena David (“Strangers with Candy”) serve as producers. The project, which will shoot on location in Kepnes’ native Cape Cod, is set for release on YouTube.
	

	”The heart of this story is a total genre clash. One minute it’s this awkward ’90s oceanside family comedy, and the next it plunges into raw psychological dread,” Kepnes said. “To pull that off, I needed a family that felt completely real and delightfully chaotic. Watching Dean, Jordan, Katherine and Audrey bring these dynamics to life as unseen terror creeps into their lives is everything I hoped it would be.”

	A release date is not yet set for “The Attentionist.”

schema.headline: Katherine Mallen Kupferer, Audrey Grace Marshall, Dean Norris, Jordan Ladd Join ‘The Attentionist’ from Caroline Kepnes (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ’30 Rock’ 20th Anniversary Reunion: Tina Fey and Tracy Morgan Try to Remember Their Lines, Alec Baldwin Riffs as Jack Donaghy and More Best Moments
description: Conan O’Brien did little to manage expectations as he kicked off Sunday evening’s “30 Rock” reunion, a one-night-only benefit at Radio City Music Ha
body:
Conan O’Brien did little to manage expectations as he kicked off Sunday evening’s “30 Rock” reunion, a one-night-only benefit at Radio City Music Hall to celebrate the beloved sitcom’s 20th anniversary.

	“Welcome to the greatest night in the history of entertainment!” he said from the stage to raucous applause. “I’m Conan O’Brien, and I’m known to exaggerate.”

	His comments didn’t seem hyperbolic to the 5,000 rowdy fans in the audience, who spent a pretty penny and braved a rainstorm for a chance to witness the live, never-to-be-televised event. Cheers from the crowd were near-deafening as O’Brien introduced the cast — Tina Fey, Alec Baldwin, Tracy Morgan and Jane Krakowski — and they kept up the enthusiasm for surprise guests like Jon Hamm, Tom Hanks, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Will Forte and Brian Williams.
	

	“What you will see tonight is, in “30 Rock” fashion, an overly ambitious grab bag of nonsense,” Fey said. Created by Fey, “30 Rock,” which ran for seven seasons on NBC from 2006-2013, takes place behind the scenes of a fictional “Saturday Night Live”-esque sketch comedy show called “TGS With Tracy Jordan.” Fey plays head writer Liz Lemon, Baldwin portrays NBC boss Jack Donaghy and Krakowski and Morgan star as cast members Jenna Maroney and Tracey Jordan.


	The cast reunion doubled as a charity fundraiser for the Boys and Girls Club of Harlem, an organization they wanted to honor for two specific reasons. “We chose the Boys and Girls of Harlem because they are a great New York institution,” Fey said. “But also because we figured we kind of owed them something because of how much Tracy Jordan struggled to shoot the commercial he did.” (In one memorable episode from Season 5, Tracy couldn’t remember his lines as he filmed a public service announcement for the Boys & Girls Clubs of America.)
	

	Before passing the mic to the cast, O’Brien took a moment to lament his too-brief role on the show (he played himself and once dated Liz Lemon) and teased Fey for casting a bunch of hot men as the boyfriends of her character.

	“After my stellar debut, I was quickly relegated to being a cheap and easy off-camera reference. I was described as merely ‘that tall, gangly, redheaded guy’ and ‘one giant lesbian,'” Conan said. “So who did get to play Liz Lemon’s love interest? I’ll tell you who. Total units like Jon Hamm, Jason Sudeikis, and Matt Damon. Drop acid much, Tina?”

	Fey revealed that Jack McBrayer was the one to suggest a 20th anniversary reunion. “He probably meant a cast dinner. But I’m not a good listener, so here we are,” Fey said. “I wanted to celebrate at Radio City because I like to feel tiny.”

	She designed the evening to be “more than just a Q&A,” stuffing the 90-minute event with elaborate musical numbers, game show sketches and other “30 Rock”-themed skits, and moments for the cast to reminisce about making the beloved comedy. 

	“No one has ever seen this show before, including us, because we have not rehearsed it,” Fey said. “But one thing I can promise you, from the bottom of my heart, we will have microphone problems.”

	If you couldn’t “go to there,” as Liz Lemon would say, Variety has compiled the best moments from the night:
	
		Tom Hanks accepts best guest star award on behalf of Elaine Stritch	

	“30 Rock” had no shortage of A-list guest stars, from Carrie Fisher (as fictional comedy writer Rosemary Howard) to Steve Martin (as Jack’s neurotic friend Gavin Volure) to Oprah Winfrey (as herself). “It was pretty wild,” said Judah Friedlander, who played “TGS” writer Frank Rossitano. “You never knew who would show up. One week it was Al Gore, and the next it could be Queen Latifah.” Katrina Bowden, who portrayed Liz’s beautiful assistant Cerie, asked: “Wait, are those real people who lived?”

	But only one bold-faced name could win the coveted “best guest star” prize, which went to Elaine Stritch as Jack’s overbearing mother Colleen Donaghy. She was (posthumously) nominated against Marcella Roy as young Liz Lemon, Sherri Shephard as Tracy’s wife Angie Jordan and Kelsey Grammer as his heist-wielding alter ego “Frajer.”
	

	“Unfortunately, Elaine can’t be here tonight to accept her award because she’s dead,” Bowden deadpanned. (Strich died in 2014 at age 89.) “So here to accept on her behalf is two-time Academy Award winner Tom Hanks.”

	Hanks was apparently tricked into attending the evening while he was one block up, near 30 Rockefeller Plaza. “I was on my way to dinner at the Rainbow Room,” Hanks said. “I eat there every night to avoid Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax.”
	
		’30 Rock’-stradomus	

	“30 Rock” is famous for predicting a bunch of stuff that proved to be bizarrely accurate. “Even though we were exhausted and writing absurdist nonsense, so much of what we wrote actually came true,” the show’s writers said from the stage. Highlights in a montage of prescient jokes include Jenna’s “free Lyle Menendez” tattoo (the brothers were recently granted an early parole hearing) and Tracy’s call with someone pretending to be Bill Cosby — “You’ve got a lot of nerve getting on the phone with me after what you did to my Aunt Paulette!” — way before the comedian was accused of drugging and sexually assaulting women. Then there was Jenna’s weight-gaining role in the fictional “Mystic Pizza: The Musical” (which now exists and began a national tour this fall) and the iconic show-within-a-show “MILF Island,” which paved the way for the very real HBO Max reality dating series “FBoy Island.”
	
		Tina and Tracy play ‘What’s my next line?’	

	McBrayer put Fey and Morgan’s memories to the test, feeding them niche quotes from the show to see if they could remember the wacky things their characters said over the course of seven seasons. They started strong; Fey knew the reason there “ain’t no party like a Liz Lemon party” because “a Liz Lemon party is mandatory.” And Morgan remembered the seminal “advice I wish I woulda got when I was your age” which was to “live every week like it’s Shark Week.”

	And then things took a turn. Fey was stumped by a clip of Liz, dressed as Princess Leia from “Star Wars” to try to get out of jury duty. “Because I can read minds?” Fey guessed. (Her actual line was “Because I’m a hologram.”) But she rebounded with her character’s memory of participating in the “Big Sister” program. (“That little girl taught me how to use a tampon.”)

	When Morgan couldn’t think of the punchline to “What is this, horseville?” he turned to the audience to supply the answer. Everyone shouted: “Because I’m surrounded by naysayers. Wordplay!” Morgan couldn’t recall other Tracy-isms, like, “I don’t get why people like brunch. What’s the benefit of combining breakdancing and lunch?” and “I was just thinking about how weird it is that we eat birds.” But he had a good excuse.
	

	“I’m supposed to remember that?” Morgan said. “You gotta give me a break. I got hit by a truck!”
	
		Dr. Leo Spaceman doles out medical advice	

	Chris Parnell’s wacky doctor Leo Spaceman, who gets promoted to Surgeon General of the United States at the end of the series, was on hand to “clear up any confusion about our official health recommendations.” A sampling of his frequently asked questions: “Do vaccines cause autism? Or, does autism cause billionaires?” (“Either way, you’re in trouble, fam.”) “Is it safe to eat lettuce yet?” (“Nope, it never was. Stick to the paleo food groups: Beef, meat, and Zyns.”) “Can I give my spouse a GLP-1 without them knowing?” (“Now, any doctor will tell you: If you don’t know the law, you can’t break it.”) That should clear a few things up!
	
		‘What would Jack Donaghy say?’	

	Since the series went off the air in 2013, “30 Rock” guest star and former “NBC Nightly News” anchor Brian Williams admitted he’s been missing Jack Donaghy’s pithy advice and commentary on the state of the world. One of the night’s sharpest sketches  — introduced by Williams — involved Jack responding to major news events of the last 13 years.

	— In 2014, Jack’s assistant Jonathan (Maulik Pancholy) told his boss that his emails were leaked in the infamous Sony hack. “The one where I tried to get Tracy in drag in the female ‘Ghostbusters’?” Jack asks, to which Jonathan replies, “No, I never sent that one. It’s the one where you offer to give Jenna to Kim Jong Un if it would help.”

	— In 2017, Kenneth, the eager page played by McBrayer, reveals he was “#MeToo’d by a lady on the camera crew.” He elaborates, saying, “She asked me what my ideal last meal would be, and I said chickpeas and Mountain Dew.’ She said, ‘Me too!’ And then we high-fived so hard, my pants fell down.”

	— In 2021, Jack shamed the insurrectionists who stormed the capitol on Jan. 6. “When I defecated on Nancy Pelosi’s desk,” he said, “I looked in her straight in the eye like a man.”

	— In 2023, Jonathan celebrated a box office rebound — “Sir, ‘Barbie’ and ‘Oppenheimer’ were a huge success. The movie business is back! — and Jack retorts: “And more importantly, now when you Google “Barbenheimer,” that’s what comes up, and not Cody Barbenheimer, the young man who mysteriously drowned in Lindsey Graham’s bathtub over Memorial Day weekend.”
	
	
		Jane Krakowski’s musical medley 	

	Fresh off her run in “Oh, Mary!” on Broadway, Krakowski wowed the room by performing several of the attention-seeking Maroney’s greatest hits. Wearing a sparkly silver dress and flanked by dancers in page uniforms, she opened with “That’s Her,” the opening theme song from “The Girlie Show” and masterfully pivoted into the feminist anthem “Muffin Top” before transitioning to Jackie Jormp-Jomp’s classic “Chunk of My Lung,” a parody of Janis Joplin’s “Piece of my Heart.” (Jenna was cast to play the music icon in an unlicensed biopic that never got off the ground.) 

	The already giddy crowd erupted when Krakowski was joined by John McEnroe to belt the “Sunday Night Football”-inspired “Tennis Night in America” and later by Forte, dressed as an angel in character as Jenna’s beau Paul L’astnamé, for a duet of the Christmas carol “O Holy Night.” Marceline Hugot, who plays Kathy Geiss, the mute daughter of GE’s boss Don Geiss, made a brief but thrilling appearance on trumpet.


	Those weren’t the only memorable musical moments. Lin-Manuel Miranda, a “30 Rock” superfan, energized the audience with the Halloween favorite “Werewolf Bar Mitzvah” before Krakowski closed out the evening with a powerful rendition of the “Rural Juror” theme song. 

	We agree: “We will never forget you!”

schema.headline: ’30 Rock’ 20th Anniversary Reunion: Tina Fey and Tracy Morgan Try to Remember Their Lines, Alec Baldwin Riffs as Jack Donaghy and More Best Moments

title: TV Cooking Shows Get Spicy With Food Influencers in the Mix: ‘It Has to Hook You In’
description: Gordon Ramsay is on set in Ireland when we speak. It’s a hot, sunny day but he is surrounded by Christmas trees and elves as he’s shooting the “Next
body:
Gordon Ramsay is on set in Ireland when we speak. It’s a hot, sunny day but he is surrounded by Christmas trees and elves as he’s shooting the “Next Level Baker” holiday special for Fox.

	It’s very festive, which seems appropriate as he’s recently uncorked the 25th season of “Hell’s Kitchen,” and earlier this year unwrapped the 10th season of “Kitchen Nightmares,” while also serving up the 16th season of the U.S. version of “MasterChef.”
	

	But despite the continued popularity of his shows, reinforced by the Netflix series about him, some in the industry are starting to ask: Have TV audiences started to lose their appetite for food shows?


	Natalie Cruz, an analyst for Ampere Analysis, says, “Globally, the commissions of reality-food shows have shown a consistent downward trend since 2022, with the highest decrease of 16% lower global commissioning volumes between 2024 to 2025, from 663 to 555 titles. This trend continues into 2026, with commissioning volumes falling by 13% between the second half of last year and the first half of this year from 282 to 245 titles.”

	Cookery shows need to add some spice to pique the hunger of audiences, according to TV sales executives. Take “The Heat,” part of the offering from international distribution and production giant ITV Studios, which folds the ingredients of a high-end cooking format in with those of a dating show. “It’s very aspirational, very glossy and escapist,” Tom Clark, ITV Studios’ executive VP global sales and commercial strategy, says.

	“The Heat” is set in a real restaurant in sun-drenched Barcelona where a group of young chefs battle it out under the supervision of a world-class Michelin chef. “The chefs are working together during the day and they’re competing, but they’re also living together at night; so they’re working hard and they’re partying hard,” Clark explains.
	

	“And what that means is the stress and the ambition for winning the cooking contest meets the relationships and the night lives that go alongside of that. What you then see is the romances, the rivalries, the flirtations, the fallouts — they all make their way back into the kitchen in the daytime.”

	Ramsay has watched the show, and he’s not impressed. “I think ‘The Heat’ is a bit of a hotch-potch … sort of ‘Big Brother’ meets ‘Top Chef.’ I was cringing watching some of the early episodes, and it just had no narrative.”

	The U.K. broadcaster ITV appeared to agree. After its first season, the show was axed.



	

					“The Heat” was a blend of cooking contest and dating show.
									“The Heat” (Courtesy of ITV Studios)
	



	Ramsay attributes the popularity of his own shows to their “live aspect,” and underscores the need to “keep things incredibly fresh.” Referring to “Hell’s Kitchen,” he says, “There’s a format, but each and every season, we rip up the rule book and rewrite the challenges.”

	The secret to its success, Ramsay says, is that he runs it like a live restaurant. “There is something magical about going into the unknown when that first ticket arrives. We train and train and train those individuals, put them through this incredible boot camp before we go live, and each and every night is a live performance, like you’d go to see in a theater,” he says.

	Lucas Green, chief content officer, operations, at Banijay Entertainment, another global TV distribution and production titan, acknowledges there has been a shift in audience tastes as food content on social media proliferates. “People love watching recipes and food porn on Instagram and TikTok, and I think that’s probably replaced the instructional cooking shows,” he says.



	

					“MasterChef” was the most adapted format in the world last year.
									Courtesy of Banijay
	



	That said, Banijay’s “MasterChef” was the most adapted format in the world last year, with versions on air in 38 territories (the total is now 41 territories), and similar formats, like “Top Chef,” are also going strong, which Green ascribes to their narrative structure.

	“[‘MasterChef’ has] got that light-touch reality storyline with people coming back week to week, and they’re very, very determined to win,” he says. “[The show] changes people’s lives. Lots of winners have gone on to get Michelin stars. It’s very aspirational.”
	

	The blending in of a story arc boosts the audience’s desire for more, encouraging binge-viewing, says Mike Beale, managing director, creative network, at ITV Studios, which has “Hell’s Kitchen” on air in 26 territories and “Come Dine With Me” in 50. “You need to take the viewer from one episode to another. Just seeing five people cook, and there’s one winner at the end of the competition, and then next week, you do the same competition again with five new people, isn’t going to do that anymore,” Beale says. “It has to hook you in and take you there, and streaming has driven that behavior.”

	Meanwhile, the networks continue to bring new zest to old favorites, such as the launch last year of “Gordon Ramsay’s Secret Service” on Fox, reinventing the “Kitchen Nightmares” formula, Olivier Levet at TV consultancy The Wit says.

	YouTube is proving to be a fertile seedbed for new cooking show concepts, Levet adds. “Content creators are experimenting with new formulas, such as battles over iconic cartoon dishes, seen in Joshua Weissman’s ‘I Tried Every Famous Cartoon Food,’ or global tournaments between typical breakfasts, with Ibai Llanos’ ‘El mundial de los desayunos,’” he says.



	

					Joshua Weissman
									Courtesy of Michael Loccisano/Getty Images for NYCWFF
	



	Meanwhile, Levet notes that the streamers have developed their own taste for cookery shows like “Dinner Time Live With David Chang,” “Culinary Class Wars,” “Iron Chef: Quest for an Iron Legend” and “The Final Table” on Netflix, and “The World Cook” on Prime Video.

	And online and linear can feed off each other, Green argues. “MasterChef” has a spin-off in Brazil, “MasterChef Creators,” which streams on YouTube, and casts only digital influencers, which has brought a younger audience to the show.

	Whatever exotic recipes the latest generation of celebrity chefs throw together, for Ramsay, his approach is simple, “I suppose I just work at keeping it fresh, and I take criticism, but I don’t sit there and self-absorb and self-obsess about how good we are. I treat every season like it’s the first.”

	And sometimes the greatest drama stirred up by Ramsay’s shows occurs after they have aired, he observes, and it’s down to a mistaken view of the realities of running a restaurant.
	

	Referring to some misguided folk on “Kitchen Nightmares,” he says, “The biggest issue I’ve got is when the program goes out and they get that fanfare and attention, especially in the media. They then get a little bit carried away with the fame. And there’s nothing famous in running a restaurant. It’s hard, brutal work that needs to be disciplined and focused on, so you can’t start indulging in success by running a restaurant and sitting down with customers and having the odd glass of champagne or drinking a martini before you start running your dining room.”

title: ABC Alleges FCC’s Attempts to Curb Its Free Speech Were Designed to Evade Judicial Review
description: ABC, in a new filing in its First Amendment lawsuit against the FCC, claims that the agency’s early-license renewal demand for its local TV stations
body:
ABC, in a new filing in its First Amendment lawsuit against the FCC, claims that the agency’s early-license renewal demand for its local TV stations was done in such a way as to circumvent “judicial review.”

	On Aug. 18, ABC sued the FCC and chairman Brendan Carr, a Trump loyalist, alleging the commission was waging an “extraordinary assault” on its First Amendment rights through the implicit threat of revoking its broadcast licenses for eight owned-and-operated stations. The FCC insists its order requiring ABC to apply for early license renewals was initiated from the agency’s investigation into alleged diversity, equity and inclusion employment practices at Disney and ABC.
	

	At an Oct. 6 hearing, Judge Loren AliKhan of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, who is hearing the case, instructed the FCC to submit a supplemental filing “on the list of alternative tools to compel discovery” in its DEI investigation into Disney and ABC other than early license renewals.


	On Monday, ABC responded to the FCC’s filing. The FCC had argued at the hearing that “‘the license renewal process is not about the licenses,’ but rather an attempt to deal with what they claim to be a discovery deficiency” in the DEI probe, the network says in the fling. “But their supplemental briefing only confirms what they conceded at the hearing: there are ‘a number of different tools’ by which the agency could have addressed the purported discovery deficiency.”

	ABC continued: “These are not merely ‘theoretical[]’ tools… they have been used by the agency for decades. Yet the agency tried none of those less intrusive tools here, instead taking the unprecedented step of calling for early license renewal of all eight ABC-owned stations at once. Defendants’ own admissions leave no doubt as to why — Defendants sought to inflict maximal coercive pressure on the media company whose speech the Administration sought to curb, while deliberately evading judicial review.”
	

	ABC has previously said that in the FCC’s DEI probe, it has produced over 11,000 pages of responsive documents “on a mutually agreed schedule” and that the agency’s Enforcement Bureau “has never suggested its existing tools are insufficient for whatever it is investigating.”

	The FCC explained to the court that using an administrative subpoena or a monetary forfeiture order to compel Disney and ABC to produce documentation in the DEI probe would require the Trump administration to seek enforcement in federal court. 

	“That Defendants openly describe judicial review as an obstacle demonstrates what Plaintiffs have been saying all along: shielding their unconstitutional campaign against ABC from judicial review is part of Defendants’ retaliatory strategy,” ABC said in its filing.

	Meanwhile, the FCC omitted several other tools at the agency’s disposal for rectifying the supposed discovery deficiency in the DEI investigation, according to ABC. First, the agency can issue cease-and-desist orders requiring a party to comply with FCC rules or orders. Second, the agency can issue formal or informal warning letters threatening consequences if a violation is not remedied. And third, the FCC can negotiate a consent decree with the broadcaster to redress any violations and resolve an enforcement matter.

	A ruling is expected once the court has reviewed the additional submissions from both parties.

	The FCC’s order in April 2026 to require ABC to file for early license renewal of its TV stations came one day after Donald Trump and Melania Trump publicly criticized a joke Jimmy Kimmel made on his show (Kimmel said Melania had “a glow like an expectant widow”) — and Trump demanded that ABC fire Kimmel. 

	On April 28, the FCC’s Media Bureau issued an order requiring Disney “to file license renewals for all of their licensed TV stations within 30 days.” The station’s licenses were otherwise not due for renewal until between 2028 and 2031. When Carr was asked at an April 30 press conference at the FCC if Kimmel’s joke would play a part in the FCC’s review of the ABC licenses, he responded that Disney is “going to have to come in and demonstrate that they’ve been operating in the public interest.”

	Separately, the FCC earlier this year initiated a formal review of whether ABC daytime talk show “The View” qualifies for an exemption to the agency’s equal-time rules for political candidates. In July, Carr said the FCC will consider ABC’s decision to not carry a live broadcast of President Trump’s speech about U.S. election security as part of its early review of its broadcast licenses.
	

	However, according to the FCC, none of those issues prompted the commission to launch an early review of the ABC licenses. In its motion seeking to have ABC’s suit dismissed, the FCC said that Carr announced the investigation into Disney and ABC’s DEI practices “long before making any of the statements about ‘The View,’ Jimmy Kimmel, or President Trump’s July 2026 public address on which Plaintiffs focus their narrative in this case.”

schema.headline: ABC Alleges FCC’s Attempts to Curb Its Free Speech Were Designed to Evade Judicial Review

            Reality TV star Kash was shot and killed in California ... just hours after sharing videos from a night out with friends ... and a woman was arrested in connection with the fatal shooting.
      
    
            The influencer -- whose real name was Mackayla Paige -- was gunned down in downtown Oakland early Sunday morning, according to local reports.
      
    
            Police say officers responded to calls of gunfire around 1:30 AM and found a woman suffering from a gunshot wound. She was rushed to a hospital, where she was pronounced dead.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Cops have arrested a woman from nearby Richmond in connection with the shooting, though they haven't released her identity or revealed what sparked the deadly confrontation.
      
    
            Making the tragedy even more heartbreaking ... Kash posted videos to her Instagram Stories Saturday night, showing herself enjoying an evening out just hours before she was killed.
      
    
            Kash appeared on several reality shows, including "Real West Coast Baddies," "RoomH8z" and "Young & Reckless."
      
    
            Her cousin, Nicky Clayton, told KTVU she was in disbelief over the killing, saying Kash had big dreams of becoming famous and starting her own business.
      
    
            A makeshift memorial honors Kash at the shooting scene ... and her death remains under investigation.
      
    
            Kash was 29.

title: Halle Berry's Son Wants To Testify In Parents' Custody Battle
description:
Halle Berry's Ex Olivier Martinez
                          Our Son Wants To Testify In Our Custody Wa
body:
Halle Berry's Ex Olivier Martinez
                          Our Son Wants To Testify In Our Custody War
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 12, 2026
                            11:47 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 12, 2026
                                12:28 PM PDT
                                    
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Olivier Martinez says his son with Halle Berry was afraid nobody would believe his abuse allegations against his mother ... so he snapped a photo to back up his story, and now he wants to testify in court.
      
    
            In new court docs, obtained by TMZ, Olivier claims their 13-year-old son Maceo took a picture of Halle following an alleged physical altercation at her home on September 26, which set off a custody war.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Olivier says Maceo had previously made allegations about his mother getting physical with him but felt nobody took his complaints seriously ... so this time, he says his son wanted photographic evidence.
      

            And that's not all ... Olivier is firing back at Halle's October 5 emergency court filing, calling it "retaliatory" and claiming she is misleading the judge about their son's medical treatment.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He claims Halle painted him as an uncooperative father who was standing in the way of Maceo's care ... even though he says their son's pediatrician and psychiatrist decided September 21 that he should not take medication at this time.
      
    
            Olivier says Halle knew about the decision and acknowledged it in writing, saying she is now pushing a "false narrative" to the court and public.
      
    
            Meanwhile, Olivier says Maceo wants to speak directly to the judge about his custody preferences and what allegedly happened at Halle's home. He argues their son deserves to tell his side before the court makes any further decisions.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... Olivier obtained a temporary restraining order after he claims Maceo told him Halle choked him during an argument over him playing a VR game.
      
    
            Halle denied the allegation, saying the two were roughhousing ... and she has since completed a court-mandated parenting program amid the bitter custody battle.
      
    
            The exes are due back in court Friday.
      
    
            We reached out to Halle's camp ... so far, no word back.

            Joe Manganiello is sidestepping the narcissist allegations, encouraging people to read his book instead of feeding into social media speculation.
      
    
            Gayle King was interviewing Joe on "CBS Mornings" when she asked the actor point-blank about Sofía Vergara's son, Manolo, posting to Instagram implying Joe's a narcissist.
      
    
            What's interesting is Joe doesn't deny being a narcissist ... simply says that's "not what the book is about."
      

            The way Joe tells it ... his memoir, "Bloodlines," isn't about his rocky relationship with Sofía, but instead about the suffering he went through during his mysterious and near-fatal health battle.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Joe claims he tried to represent everyone in the book with "an amount of grace" -- although he did make some pretty harsh allegations about the way his ex-wife allegedly treated him during his illness.
      
    
            But Joe insists the discussion is a "nuanced" one that he doesn't want to air out on social media ... seemingly firing back at Sofía and Manolo.
      
    
            Joe's book is out tomorrow ... and he's doing all he can to drum up interest.
